Volume 17 · Chapter 02

Explaining intuition, mathematics and evidence

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v17-c01

By the endTeach a concept across levels without changing its meaning or hiding assumptions.

Volume 17 · Chapter 2

Explaining intuition, mathematics and evidence

Capability. Teach the same economic idea in ordinary language, notation, a table and an evidence statement while preserving its target and assumptions. A learner should be able to move between those forms, identify where an analogy fails and explain a changed example without merely copying the original calculation.

Prerequisites. Use the objective–evidence alignment in learning objectives and prerequisite design. The economic inputs are proportional change, ratios and conditional reasoning from the common core; the second lesson uses the finite-roster assignment argument taught in identification. This chapter supplies that argument again in full. Its lessons and learner responses are invented teaching specimens. No class has been observed, no learner gain measured and no teaching efficacy established by producing these pages.

1. Preserve the claim when you change the representation

“Make it intuitive” should not mean replacing a conditional result with a stronger slogan. An explanation can be short and still name its object, comparison and crucial condition. A representation is a form in which the same relationship is expressed: words, symbols, a numerical table or a diagram. An analogy borrows a familiar setting to illuminate part of that relationship. The analogy is useful only to the extent that its mapped relations agree with the target concept. A resemblance in appearance is not a proof.

Before teaching, write a small translation contract: what is the quantity, what changes, what stays fixed, and what would count as evidence that the learner understands? Keep its meaning in every version. Define each symbol when it first enters, with units and domain. Say whether a number is an input, an accounting consequence, a model implication or an empirical estimate. Ask the learner to translate back: “Which term in the equation corresponds to that sentence?” A fluent recitation can coexist with the wrong denominator or causal target.

The Institute of Education Sciences' September 2007 practice-guide page recommends connecting concrete and abstract forms, pairing graphical with verbal explanations, and alternating worked examples with problem solving; it labels these recommendations as supported by moderate evidence. That is a synthesis and recommendation, not a trial of the lessons here or a guarantee for every learner. We implement a bounded version: a complete example, an explicit connection between forms, then a changed task with reasoning. The CMU alignment guidance supports matching practice and assessment to the intended capability. Here, the assessed capability is explanation and translation, so an answer must do more than produce a number.

There is no requirement to display every form at once. Introduce a manageable object, connect the next representation explicitly, and remove an unnecessary picture or symbol if it is doing no explanatory work. Provide the spoken content in writing, define table headings and describe the relevant pattern without relying on color. Check prerequisite understanding with a small task rather than assuming that a learner's vocabulary reveals it. These are proposed design choices for these lessons; evaluate them through actual learner work and revise when they fail.

2. Mini-lesson: a larger money balance can buy fewer baskets

Case 1 — Purchasing capacity, not disappearing money

Objective and first check. Given two positive prices for the same fixed basket and two money balances, calculate the change in purchasing capacity and explain why nominal growth alone is insufficient. Ask first: “If one basket costs 2 currency units and you have 10, how many whole-or-fractional basket units can the balance buy?” The answer is 5. A learner who multiplies needs the division/units relationship repaired before the growth formula. We allow fractional baskets as a measuring unit; this is not an indivisible shopping problem.

Complete spoken opening. “At the beginning, you can use 200 currency units to buy 100 units of this fixed basket, because each costs 2. Later you have 220, but each identical basket costs 2.50. The balance can then buy 88 baskets. You have more money and less purchasing capacity. Nothing in this calculation says that money vanished. The question is how much of the same basket the balance can command at each date.” The numbers are original and hypothetical; this is not a current inflation or investment example.

Case 1 complete inputs and purchasing-capacity calculation
DateMoney M, currency unitsBasket price P, currency per basketCapacity Q=M/P, baskets
02002100
12202.588

Notation and domain. M₀>0 is the initial money balance; M₁≥0 is the final balance. P₀,P₁>0 price exactly the same basket in the same currency. Qₜ=Mₜ/Pₜ is potential purchasing capacity, not necessarily actual consumption. Units cancel: currency ÷ (currency/basket)=baskets. Define nominal balance growth r=(M₁−M₀)/M₀, basket-price growth π=(P₁−P₀)/P₀ and purchasing-capacity growth g=(Q₁−Q₀)/Q₀. Thus r≥−1 and π>−1. Dates, basket composition and quality are held comparable; there are no fees or other uses of the balance hidden in the calculation.

Derivation, with the verbal bridge. From the definitions, M₁=M₀(1+r) and P₁=P₀(1+π). Therefore Q₁/Q₀=(M₁/P₁)/(M₀/P₀)=(1+r)/(1+π), and

g=(1+r)/(1+π)−1=(r−π)/(1+π).

“The numerator of the ratio says how many times larger the money balance became; its denominator says how many times dearer the basket became. Dividing the multipliers compares the two purchasing capacities.” Substitution gives (1/10,1/4,-3/25) for (r,π,g):10%,25%,−12%. The capacity change is−12 baskets from a 100-basket baseline. Saying “down 12 percentage points” without identifying the compared rates would confuse a growth rate with a difference between growth rates.

A table is a conditional comparison. Hold final money at 220 and vary only its basket price. Read the next table across rows as a counterfactual exercise; it is not a historical price path or evidence that income stayed fixed in an actual economy.

Holding M=220 fixed: the denominator changes capacity
Price, currency/basketPurchasing capacity, baskets
2110
2.2100
2.588

The pattern is decreasing: for M>0 and P′>P>0, dividing the same positive M by the larger denominator gives M/P′<M/P. At M=0, capacity is zero at either price. This order argument proves the claimed direction over the full stated domain; it does not require a drawing or a fitted trend.

Misleading analogy and repair. A proposed slide calls inflation “a hole that leaks 25% of the money out of a bucket.” That would reduce a 220 balance to 165 and suggests a cash outflow which the table does not contain. Replace it with: “Think of money as tokens and the basket price as tokens required per basket. More tokens help, but a higher token requirement can more than offset them. Count baskets by dividing; the tokens themselves need not disappear.” The mapping is money↔tokens, price↔tokens per basket, capacity↔baskets. The analogy does not establish how basket quality, substitution, borrowing, taxes or preferences change welfare. If any of those is the question, state a new target and model.

Respond to a synthetic learner's reasoning. Learner: “I used 10−25=−15%, so the final capacity is 85.” Instructor: “Your subtraction compares the two growth rates, but those rates act on different denominators. What is 220 divided by 2.50?” Learner: “88.” Instructor: “Then compare 88 with the initial 100. The exact loss is 12%. Subtraction is a small-rate approximation, not an identity. Here it misses growth by 3 percentage points.” Algebra makes the approximation error visible:

g−(r−π)=−π(r−π)/(1+π).

At the supplied values this is 3/100. No fixed tolerance is promised by the word “small”; calculate the error or state an acceptable tolerance for the application. If r=π, g=0 exactly. If π=0, g=r exactly. If M₁=0, then r=−1 and g=−1 whatever admissible price change occurs. A zero or negative basket price is outside this calculation.

Evidence interpretation and check for understanding. A verified record of the two balances and two basket prices would establish the computed capacity change for that basket, subject to measurement. It would not show what the person bought, whether the basket matched their needs, why prices changed, or the causal effect of a policy. Ask: “Could actual consumption rise even when this balance's capacity falls?” Yes: other income, borrowing, savings or a changed purchase basket could matter; those lie outside this two-balance calculation. A successful answer preserves the defined target instead of claiming that the formula measures welfare.

3. Mini-lesson: a randomized contrast is not a guaranteed causal answer in one draw

Case 2 — Explain the experiment before interpreting its table

Objective and contrast. Explain why a uniformly randomized difference in group means targets an average offer effect, while one realized contrast can differ from that effect. Four banks form the entire teaching roster. Offer Z=1 means a specified refinancing-information invitation; Z=0 means no invitation. Outcome Y=1 means the bank's six-month lending stock is at least its baseline stock under a fixed bank perimeter, and 0 means it is below baseline. Consistency means the observed outcome equals that bank's potential outcome under its assigned offer. No interference means one bank's outcome does not depend on the others' offers. The invitation is the treatment; attendance, borrower credit and welfare are different targets.

The next table is an invented complete potential-outcome schedule for instruction. Yᵢ(0) and Yᵢ(1) describe what bank i would do under each offer status. A real experiment normally observes only one of these for each bank. Showing both in a teaching construction is a way to inspect the estimator; it is not a claim that an actual analyst sees both counterfactuals.

Complete synthetic potential outcomes, fixed across assignment draws
BankY(0), no invitationY(1), invitationIndividual effect
A011
B000
C110
D110

The finite-roster average effect is τ=(1/4)Σᵢ[Yᵢ(1)−Yᵢ(0)]=1/4, or 25 percentage points on this binary outcome. The proportion scale is dimensionless; the difference is a difference in probabilities/proportions, not a 25% proportional increase from a specified initial rate. The experiment uniformly chooses two of the four banks for invitation, so there are six equally likely unordered pairs.

Complete novice-facing explanation. “We can see all the possible outcomes because we invented this little world. Only A changes when offered the invitation. Averaging one change across four banks gives an effect of one quarter. Now imagine running its lottery. If A and B get the offer, one of those two succeeds; both controls C and D succeed. The observed offered-minus-control difference is one half minus one, or minus one half. That negative comparison does not mean the arithmetic of our positive average effect failed. The lottery happened to put the two banks that otherwise fail together in the offered group.”

One realized assignment: invite A and B
GroupObserved successesObserved banksSuccess proportion
Invited A,B121/2
Control C,D221

The realized difference is -1/2, or−50 percentage points. The true effect in the complete teaching schedule is+25 points. These compare two different objects: a random estimator value and the fixed target it estimates. Neither is an attendance effect.

All possible invitation pairs under the uniform lottery
Invited pairOffered-minus-control proportion
A,B−1/2
A,C1/2
A,D1/2
B,C0
B,D0
C,D1

The average over the six equally likely values is 1/4. This is an exact enumeration, not a simulation or a large-sample approximation. It does not supply a confidence interval for an unknown real-world effect.

General derivation at a more mathematical level. For an even fixed roster size N≥2, assign n=N/2 invitations uniformly without replacement. Treat all potential outcomes as fixed. Let Zᵢ be the 0/1 assignment indicator and define

τ=N⁻¹Σᵢ[Yᵢ(1)−Yᵢ(0)],   Δ̂=n⁻¹ΣᵢZᵢYᵢ(1)−(N−n)⁻¹Σᵢ(1−Zᵢ)Yᵢ(0).

Here Δ̂ is the random offered-minus-control contrast, Σᵢ means sum over all roster banks, and E[·] means average over the assignment lottery. Each bank appears in the offered group with probability n/N. Linearity of expectation gives E[n⁻¹ΣZᵢYᵢ(1)]=n⁻¹Σ(n/N)Yᵢ(1)=N⁻¹ΣYᵢ(1). Likewise E[(N−n)⁻¹Σ(1−Zᵢ)Yᵢ(0)]=N⁻¹ΣYᵢ(0). Subtracting gives E[Δ̂]=τ. Independence between assignment indicators is unnecessary: fixed group size makes them dependent, and linearity still applies. The argument requires the stated assignment probabilities and consistent, fully observed outcomes under the defined no-interference target. It does not prove the same claim after selected attendance, missing outcomes or a changed assignment rule.

Repair a tempting analogy. “Randomization deals two identical hands” is false. It gives a specified chance to each allocation; it does not make the realized groups identical in baseline risk or realized outcomes. A better card analogy is a fair shuffle with fixed hand sizes: each bank-card has the same chance of entering the offered hand, yet one hand may contain more high-baseline banks. The mapping is bank↔card, assignment↔hand and lottery↔shuffle. A card's fixed suit is not a model of the treatment effect: each bank has two potential outcomes, and the offer determines which is seen. Stop the analogy there and return to the potential-outcome table.

Respond to a second synthetic learner. Learner: “The table says−50 points, so the invitation caused harm in these banks.” Instructor: “Which number is observed and which averages both potential outcomes? Show the two sums.” Learner: “Observed means are 1/2 and 1; the four effects are 1,0,0,0.” Instructor: “Exactly. The first contrast is−1/2, while the target is 1/4 in our invented complete schedule. A real analyst would not know that full schedule. Random assignment justifies the estimator's expectation under the design, not reading a single noisy comparison as the target with certainty.” A further check asks the learner to reconstruct the A,C allocation, obtaining+1/2, and explain why changing the lottery could change the expectation.

Empirical reading. In an actual study, first establish the assignment process, treatment definition, outcome completeness and measurement, then choose inference appropriate to the design. A positive or negative sample difference alone does not establish the true sign, receipt effects, a mechanism or a target-population effect. The exact artificial schedule teaches one design property. It is neither empirical evidence about refinancing nor a claim that randomization guarantees precision, external validity or ethical authorization.

4. Use learner work to decide what to explain next

An incorrect answer can arise from different steps. “−15%” in Case 1 may reflect a remembered approximation; “20” in the five-basket prerequisite may reflect multiplication instead of division; a claim of welfare may reflect a target error despite correct arithmetic. Ask the learner to state the denominator, show a numerical check and say what the answer measures. Respond to that reasoning, then give a changed case that could expose the same error. Do not infer mastery from the learner agreeing with your correction.

A compact sequence for these lessons is: name the target in words; demonstrate a complete case; define notation as a compression of that case; derive the relationship; compare the table with the algebra; then ask the learner to explain a changed input or assumption. The evidence of learning is the learner's unaided reconstruction and boundary explanation, not the instructor's smooth delivery. Have a second reader check that a simplified version has not silently dropped a condition. For example, “higher prices reduce capacity” must hold the money balance and basket fixed; “randomized comparisons are unbiased” must specify the assignment rule and the target.

For an unfamiliar context, apply the same discipline to a supplied identity. If starting cash is C₀, receipts are I and payments are O, all in common currency over one period, and these are the only cash movements, then C₁=C₀+I−O. The end stock, inflows and net change are different objects. Cash receipts do not by themselves define accounting profit; no revenue/expense recognition information has been supplied. A small table and a sentence can preserve those distinctions more usefully than an unexplained label such as “cash is king.”

5. Exercises

  1. Keep Case 1's initial money 200 and basket price 2, but set final money to 240 and final price to 2.4. Calculate both capacities, r,π and g. Write a two-sentence explanation for a learner who thinks any positive nominal growth means greater purchasing capacity.
  2. Using fixed final money 220, construct a price/capacity table for prices (2,2.75,4). Write the sentence that makes its held-fixed comparison explicit and explain why a collection of observed households at those prices would not automatically test the same relationship.
  3. For r=0.05 and π=0.02, calculate exact purchasing-capacity growth, the subtraction approximation and their difference in percentage points. Explain the special cases π=0,r=π and r=−1. Replace the leaky-bucket analogy with a complete accurate three-sentence explanation.
  4. A synthetic learner writes: “The balance grew 10%, prices rose 25%, so actual consumption and welfare fell 12% because inflation removed money.” Write a corrective response that preserves the correct arithmetic, identifies three distinct unsupported interpretations and asks a changed understanding-check question with its expected answer.
  5. Use the full potential-outcome schedule in Case 2. Reconstruct the observed outcomes and contrast when A,C are invited. Compute the roster effect directly and explain, in one complete paragraph, why these two numbers need not be equal even though assignment is randomized.
  6. Change only the lottery: A is always invited, and one of B,C,D is chosen uniformly for the second invitation. Calculate the expected unweighted offered-minus-control contrast from the three possible pairs and compare it with τ. Identify the step of the general proof that no longer works, and write a corrected claim for this changed design.
  7. Write a complete short response to a learner who says: “A fair shuffle makes the groups identical, and dependent assignment indicators invalidate your expectation proof.” Use the actual tables and one line of algebra; state the analogy's useful mapping and its limit. Give a follow-up check and its answer.
  8. Teach the cash identity from Section 4 using (40,80,70) for (C₀,I,O). Supply a three-row table of starting stock, net change and ending stock; derive the result; write a novice explanation and a precise technical sentence. Respond to “receipts 80 means profit 80,” and name a condition under which the supplied identity would be incomplete.
Complete solutions and evaluation guidance

1. Equal multipliers preserve capacity

Initial capacity is 200/2=100 and final is 240/2.4=100. Rates are r=1/5,π=1/5,g=0; the complete vector is (100,100,1/5,1/5,0). “The money balance and the price of the same basket both grew 20%, so their common multiplier cancels. The balance buys 100 baskets at either date, so nominal growth alone has not increased this basket's purchasing capacity.” Full credit requires both division calculations, the ratio identity and the held-fixed basket, without claiming unchanged actual consumption or welfare.

2. A conditional table needs a conditional sentence

Capacity of a fixed 220 balance
PriceCapacity
2110
2.7580
455

The capacities are (110,80,55) baskets. “Holding money at 220 and the basket definition fixed, a higher price per basket reduces the number of baskets that balance can buy.” Different households may have different money balances, basket definitions and other resources; a cross-household association does not hold these fixed automatically. If measured M and P are used to construct Q=M/P, matching that identity checks consistency of the construction, not a causal price experiment. Grade the complete table, units, conditional sentence and the distinction between an identity and empirical identification.

3. Quantify an approximation rather than rename it exact

Exact g=(1.05/1.02)−1=1/34≈2.941176%; subtraction gives 3/100=3%. Exact minus approximate is−1/1700 as a proportion, or−1/17 percentage points≈−0.058824. Thus (1/34,3/100,-1/17) records exact, approximate and the point difference. If π=0 then g=r; if r=π then g=0; if r=−1 then g=−1 for every π>−1. “A balance is a number of tokens, and the basket price tells us how many tokens each basket requires. Divide the balance by that price at each date and compare the resulting basket counts. A higher price need not remove tokens, and subtracting the two growth rates is only an approximation to this division.” Credit exact arithmetic and units, all three boundaries, and an analogy that preserves the mapping and does not imply an actual cash leak.

4. Repair meaning without discarding a correct calculation

“Your−12% is the change in the purchasing capacity of the specified balance for the same basket. It is not a measured change in actual consumption, since purchases and other resources were not observed; it is not a welfare change, since preferences and relevant alternatives were not specified; and it is not evidence that money physically disappeared or that a policy caused the change. The nominal balance actually rose from 200 to 220. Try this changed check: if the price instead stayed 2 while money rose to 220, what could this balance buy, and what would remain unknown?” The answer is 110 baskets, a 10% capacity gain; actual purchases, welfare and the cause of the money change remain unknown. Grade preservation of valid arithmetic, all three unsupported meanings and a complete changed check/answer.

5. Separate a random comparison from its target

A,C reveal Y_A(1)=1 and Y_C(1)=1; controls B,D reveal Y_B(0)=0 and Y_D(0)=1. The observed means are 1 and 1/2, difference 1/2. The full schedule's effects remain(1,0,0,0), with average 1/4. The contrast and target are (1/2,1/4). “Randomization gives each two-bank pair the specified chance; it does not force the two realized baseline-outcome distributions to match. Our observed contrast in this draw is one half, but averaging the estimator across all six pairs gives one quarter, equal to the fixed roster effect. The full potential-outcome table is available only because this is an invented lesson, so a real analyst cannot simply replace an estimate with the known teaching target.” Credit all four revealed outcomes, both averages and the complete design-versus-realization explanation.

6. Changing assignment changes the argument

The permitted pairs are A,B; A,C; A,D, with contrasts−1/2,1/2,1/2. Their mean is 1/6, not the roster effect 1/4; the bias is−1/12. The checked values are (1/6,1/4,-1/12). Now P(Z_A=1)=1 and the other inclusion probabilities are 1/3, not n/N=1/2. Consequently n⁻¹ΣE[Zᵢ]Yᵢ(1) cannot be replaced by N⁻¹ΣYᵢ(1), and the control expectation changes too. “Under this altered lottery the unweighted difference has expected value 1/6 in the supplied schedule; it is not an unbiased estimator of this roster's 1/4 effect. An alternative estimator or target would need a new argument, and A's never-observed untreated outcome is a support problem for design-based recovery of the full-roster effect without additional information.” Full credit includes actual pair calculations, the failed inclusion-probability step and a bounded replacement claim, not merely the word ‘bias.’

7. A fair lottery does not promise identical groups

“A uniform shuffle gives every bank the same invitation probability, but the A,B draw puts two banks with zero untreated outcomes together while C,D both have untreated outcome 1. Groups therefore need not be identical. The fixed two-bank invitation count makes the Z indicators dependent; nevertheless E[ΣZᵢYᵢ(1)]=ΣE[Zᵢ]Yᵢ(1) by linearity, which does not require independence. The card analogy maps banks to cards and group assignment to hands; it does not encode each bank's two potential outcomes as an unchanging suit.” Follow-up: “Under the original lottery, what is P(Z_A=1), and does knowing Z_B=1 leave it unchanged?” Answers are 1/2 and no: conditional on B being invited, one of A,C,D is selected, so P(Z_A=1|Z_B=1)=1/3. The two probabilities are (1/2,1/3). Grade the actual counterexample, valid algebra, mapping/limit and complete conditional-probability check.

8. Carry a new identity across forms

Cash reconciliation, common currency units
ObjectAmount
Starting stock C₀40
Net cash change I−O10
Ending stock C₁50

C₁=40+80−70=50; change=10. The checked pair is (10,50). Novice explanation: “Begin with 40 in cash, add the 80 that arrives and subtract the 70 that leaves. The balance grows by 10 to 50; incoming money and money left over are different amounts.” Technical sentence: “Over the specified period with no other cash movements, the closing cash stock equals the opening stock plus receipts minus payments, all in common currency.” Reply: “Receipts 80 records cash inflow, not profit; we need information about which amounts are recognized revenue and expense before calculating profit.” If there is an omitted owner contribution, currency revaluation or other balance change, the stated cash-movement list is incomplete and must be extended; do not silently force the residual into sales. Credit the table/derivation, both explanations, the stock/flow/profit boundary and a concrete omitted component.

6. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In a short explanation to a peer, move from the Case 1 table to its growth formula and back, then explain why the randomized contrast's expectation is a different statement from its value in one draw. Ask the peer to change one input and one assumption. Retain the exact questions and responses; reading the model answer aloud is practice, not independent teaching evidence.

Teach-back answer guide

A complete explanation names baskets as the capacity unit, derives the ratio of nominal and price multipliers, and states same-basket/positive-price conditions. It then names the fixed potential-outcome target, the random group contrast and equal inclusion probabilities; the six-pair average agrees with the target although individual contrasts differ. A changed price tests division, while a changed assignment rule tests the expectation proof. Successful feedback identifies the learner's reasoning and asks a new check; it does not merely repeat the original answer. A real evaluator should judge clarity, correctness and the learner's actual response, without treating this scripted specimen as a classroom observation.

Delayed task. After a study interval, without the examples, use balances 150→165 and fixed-basket prices 3→3.3. Explain the capacity result in words and algebra. Then explain why the statement “a randomized difference is unbiased” cannot justify an attendance-only comparison. Finally repair the phrase “inflation steals the money” without denying that a higher price can reduce capacity when money is held fixed.

Delayed answer guide

Both capacities are 50 baskets; both balance and price grow 10%, so g=1.1/1.1−1=0. An attendance-only comparison conditions on a subsequent choice and need not retain the original random assignment probabilities or target; it requires a separate identification argument. “Inflation changes how much of the basket a given balance can buy; it is not itself a recorded withdrawal from that balance.” Full credit preserves the basket, denominator and assignment/receipt distinctions in the new setting. If the learner already studied this answer, change both values and one assumption and independently verify the new key.

Deeper study and next step. These two lessons show how to preserve a claim across forms; they do not establish which teaching sequence works best for every audience, how to estimate actual learning gains, or how to infer a real study's treatment effect. Use observed learner work and appropriate teaching evidence to revise your explanations. The next chapter, designing an undergraduate economics course, places such lessons inside a complete sequence of objectives, practice and assessment.
